Option D ignores the team's empirical velocity data in favor of speculative individual estimates.
options: Use the highest recorded velocity of 24 points to give the product owner the most optimistic forecast, ensuring stakeholder confidence by presenting the best-case completion scenario as the baseline plan

Ask each team member to estimate their individual remaining capacity and sum the results for a bottom-up forecast, using individual productivity rates rather than team-level velocity to improve accuracy
Use the velocity range to provide a probabilistic forecast: best case five sprints at 24 points per sprint, most likely six sprints at 20 points, worst case eight sprints at 15 points
Use the average velocity of 20 points per sprint and provide a single-point forecast of six sprints remaining, presenting this as a definitive commitment to stakeholders for planning purposes

data.stem: A project manager completed a complex IT infrastructure project six months ago. The project met all its objectives on time and within budget. However, the benefits realization review shows that only 40% of expected business benefits have been achieved. What is the most likely cause?
data.explanation: When a project delivers on scope, time, and budget but benefits are not realized, the gap is typically in organizational adoption. Option A is contradicted by the project meeting objectives. Option C is contradicted by on-time, in-budget delivery. Option D is possible but less likely given the project met its objectives. Insufficient change management is the most common cause of the delivery-benefit gap.
options: Organizational change management was insufficient, resulting in low adoption of the new infrastructure capabilities
The project scope was inadequately defined during planning, leading to misaligned deliverables and unmet expectations
The project team lacked the technical skills to deliver the right solution, resulting in a product that failed to meet requirements
The benefits were overestimated in the original business case, causing a gap between projected and realized value

data.stem: A project manager discovers that a key stakeholder has been providing conflicting direction to different team members, causing confusion and rework. When confronted, the stakeholder insists they have been consistent. The project manager has email evidence of the contradictions. What is the best approach?
options: Escalate the issue to the project sponsor with the email evidence and request that the stakeholder be removed from direct team communication
Implement a communication plan that routes all stakeholder direction through the project manager to prevent conflicting guidance
Present the contradictory emails in a team meeting to establish a single source of truth and prevent future occurrences
Share the contradictory communications privately with the stakeholder, seek to understand their perspective, and establish a formal change request process for future direction changes
data.explanation: Private discussion preserves the relationship while addressing the issue with evidence. Establishing a formal process prevents recurrence without being confrontational. Option A publicly embarrasses the stakeholder and damages the relationship. Option C escalates prematurely without attempting direct resolution. Option D creates a communication bottleneck and doesn't address the underlying issue with the stakeholder.

data.stem: An organization is implementing a new project governance policy that requires all projects to conduct AI impact assessments before using any AI or machine learning components. A project manager has a project already in flight that uses three AI components, none of which had impact assessments. The policy states it applies to all active projects. How should the project manager proceed?
data.explanation: When a policy applies to active projects, compliance must be achieved. Option A attempts to avoid compliance. Option C is an overreaction. Option D delays compliance. Conducting retroactive assessments addresses the governance requirement while maintaining the project's AI capabilities.
options: Remove the AI components from the project to avoid the assessment requirement entirely, replacing them with traditional rule-based alternatives
Conduct retroactive AI impact assessments for all three components and integrate the results into the project's governance documentation
Request a grandfather clause exemption since the AI components were implemented before the policy was enacted, and document the exemption request in the project log
Acknowledge the policy in the project status report but defer the assessments until the next project phase when dedicated compliance resources become available

data.stem: A construction project manager calculates that the critical path runs through activities A-C-F-H-J with a total duration of 45 days. A senior engineer reports that Activity F can be shortened by 5 days if a specialized crew is brought in at an additional cost of $20,000. The project has a $50,000 schedule contingency reserve. What additional information does the project manager need before making this decision?
options: Whether the project schedule has been baselined and whether change requests require CCB approval
Whether the specialized crew is available and whether the project sponsor approves overtime work
Whether the $20,000 cost is within the project manager's approval authority and whether shortening F changes the critical path
Whether Activity F has any float and whether the total project budget can absorb the cost
data.explanation: Two critical considerations: (1) approval authority — the PM needs to know if they can authorize $20,000, and (2) whether shortening F by 5 days might cause a near-critical path to become the new critical path, negating the benefit. Option B focuses on logistics prematurely. Option C is incorrect because F is on the critical path and therefore has zero float. Option D addresses process but not the technical and financial analysis needed.

data.stem: A project sponsor asks the project manager to skip the formal change control process for a scope change because 'it's a small change and the CCB meeting is two weeks away.' The change involves adding a data export feature requested by the largest client. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: Governance processes exist for good reasons but should include mechanisms for urgency. Option A bypasses governance. Option B is rigid without exploring alternatives. Option D implements without authorization. Explaining the process while exploring expedited review balances governance integrity with responsiveness.
options: Explain the importance of change control, assess whether the change qualifies for expedited review, and follow the appropriate process
Deny the change outright and tell the sponsor to wait for the next CCB meeting, regardless of the urgency or business impact of the requested modification
Accommodate the sponsor's request immediately since maintaining the sponsor relationship is critical to project success and outweighs formal change evaluation
Implement the change but document it retroactively at the next CCB meeting, accepting the risk of bypassing the established change control governance process

data.stem: A scrum team is developing a mobile banking application. The product owner has defined a product goal and created an initial backlog. During the first sprint planning session, the team identifies that several user stories have unclear acceptance criteria and dependencies on an external payment gateway API that has not been finalized. What should the team do?
options: Split the unclear stories into technical spikes and implementation stories, placing only the spikes in the first sprint
Include all stories in the sprint and work with the payment gateway vendor during the sprint to clarify the API
Delay the first sprint until all acceptance criteria are defined and the external API is finalized
Pull only the stories with clear acceptance criteria and no external dependencies into the first sprint, and refine the remaining stories for future sprints
data.explanation: The team should only commit to stories that meet the definition of ready — clear acceptance criteria and manageable dependencies. Unclear stories should be refined further. Option B commits to uncertain work, risking sprint failure. Option C delays delivery unnecessarily when ready stories exist. Option D forces all unclear items into spikes, which may be premature — some stories may simply need refinement, not research.

data.stem: A project manager leading a product development project in an agile environment learns that a key competitor has filed a patent that may overlap with one of the product's core features. The feature is currently in development. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: External business environment changes (competitor patent) require proper evaluation. Option A ignores a real risk. Option B overreacts without legal analysis. Option D attempts a solution without understanding the legal implications. Engaging legal while continuing other work balances risk management with productivity.
options: Continue development since the patent has only been filed and not yet granted, and monitor the patent office proceedings to determine if any action becomes necessary later
Redesign the feature to work differently from the patented approach without consulting legal counsel, assuming that a sufficiently different implementation will avoid infringement
Engage the organization's legal team to assess the patent risk, inform the product owner, and develop contingency plans while development continues on other features
Remove the feature from the product backlog entirely to avoid any potential legal issues, without first assessing the actual risk level or exploring alternative implementations

data.stem: A project manager working in a regulated pharmaceutical environment is managing a drug development project. The FDA issues new guidance requiring additional clinical trial documentation. The project's change control board meets bi-weekly. The next meeting is in 10 days, but the new requirement affects work currently in progress. What should the project manager do?
options: Invoke the emergency change process to get expedited approval and begin incorporating the requirement
Ask the team to informally begin the additional documentation while waiting for formal approval
Implement the new documentation requirement immediately since regulatory compliance cannot wait
Wait for the next change control board meeting to formally address the new requirement
data.explanation: Regulatory compliance is urgent but still requires governance. Option A risks non-compliance. Option B bypasses governance entirely. Option D creates informal work without authorization. The emergency change process provides the mechanism for urgent changes while maintaining governance integrity.

data.stem: A project manager is managing a large agile program with five scrum teams. The organization's new continuous improvement policy requires all teams to track and report improvement metrics quarterly. Three of the five teams view this as bureaucratic overhead that slows them down. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: Continuous improvement policies should be implemented in ways that align with the team's working methods. Option A undermines organizational policy. Option B ignores valid concerns about overhead. Option D escalates instead of problem-solving. Finding lightweight, integrated metrics satisfies the policy while respecting agile principles.
options: Exempt the three resistant teams from the reporting requirement to maintain their velocity, setting a precedent that teams can opt out of organizational policies
Enforce the policy strictly and address any velocity decline through additional resources or extended timelines, ensuring uniform compliance across all teams
Escalate the teams' resistance to senior management for resolution, requesting that leadership mandate compliance with the standardized reporting policy
Work with the teams to identify lightweight metrics that satisfy the policy while integrating naturally into their existing agile ceremonies

data.stem: A project manager is running a kanban-based maintenance project for a legacy system. The team has a work-in-progress limit of 5 items. Recently, urgent compliance fixes have been consuming 3-4 of those slots consistently, leaving little capacity for planned improvements. What is the best approach?
data.explanation: Continuous improvement means addressing root causes, not just symptoms. Option A masks the problem by increasing WIP. Option B deprioritizes compliance. Option D adds resources without understanding why compliance issues are recurring. Root cause analysis combined with a structured expedite lane addresses both the immediate capacity issue and the underlying problem.
options: Analyze the root causes of recurring compliance issues to reduce their frequency, and establish a separate expedite lane for genuine compliance emergencies
Increase the WIP limit to 8 to accommodate both compliance fixes and planned improvements simultaneously, allowing more items to be in progress at any given time
Hire additional team members to handle the compliance workload separately, creating a dedicated compliance squad that operates independently from the main team
Prioritize planned improvements over compliance fixes to maintain the improvement roadmap, deferring compliance items to a dedicated remediation sprint at the end of the quarter

data.stem: An agile team has been asked to provide a fixed-price bid for a client project. The product backlog has been estimated at 400 story points, and the team's historical velocity is 25 points per sprint at a cost of $50,000 per sprint. The project manager must include financial contingency in the bid. What is the most appropriate approach?
data.explanation: Fixed-price agile work carries uncertainty from scope discovery, estimation variance, and team productivity fluctuations. A contingency buffer (typically 15-30%) is appropriate for risk coverage. Option A provides no margin for uncertainty. Option C is dogmatic — agile can work with fixed-price constraints with proper planning. Option D effectively makes it a time-and-materials contract disguised as fixed-price.
options: Bid exactly $800,000 (16 sprints x $50,000) since using historical velocity provides an accurate estimate, and include this as a firm fixed-price commitment with no contingency allowance
Bid $800,000 but include a clause allowing unlimited change orders at the team's hourly rate, effectively converting the fixed-price bid into a time-and-materials arrangement if scope changes
Bid $1,000,000 by adding a 25% contingency buffer to account for the inherent uncertainty in fixed-price agile work and the risk of scope discovery during execution
Refuse to provide a fixed-price bid since agile methodologies are incompatible with fixed-price contracts, and recommend the client adopt a time-and-materials arrangement instead of a fixed bid

data.stem: A project manager is managing a software project where the team implemented a continuous integration/continuous deployment pipeline as part of the quality management plan. The pipeline automatically rejects code that does not meet defined quality standards. A developer complains that the automated quality gates are slowing their productivity. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: A data-driven approach examines which quality gates add value and which create unnecessary friction. Some checks may be redundant or poorly configured. Optimizing rather than removing or rigidly maintaining gates balances quality with productivity. Option A creates inconsistent quality standards. Option C ignores legitimate process improvement. Option D abdicates the PM's responsibility for process management.
options: Analyze the data on rejection rates and reasons, then work with the team to optimize the quality gates by removing unnecessary checks while keeping those that catch genuine defects

Maintain all quality gates as-is since any relaxation of quality standards creates unacceptable risk, and inform the team that the current false positive rate is an acceptable cost of quality assurance
Remove the automated quality gates for experienced developers who have a track record of high-quality code, implementing a tiered review system based on individual developer performance history

Escalate the complaint to the quality assurance manager since quality processes are outside the project manager's authority, and defer any changes to the quality gates until a formal review is conducted

data.stem: A project manager is managing scope for an agile project delivering a logistics platform. The product owner wants to add a new real-time tracking feature that was not in the original product vision. The feature would require integrating with a third-party GPS provider and would take approximately three sprints. What should the project manager facilitate?
data.explanation: In agile, scope changes are expected and welcomed if they deliver value. The project manager should facilitate an informed prioritization decision, weighing the new feature against existing backlog items. Option A applies a predictive mindset to an agile project. Option B disrupts the current sprint without proper analysis. Option D assumes no existing work can be deprioritized to accommodate the new feature.
options: Add the feature immediately to the current sprint to demonstrate agile flexibility and responsiveness to stakeholder feedback, even though it will disrupt the team's existing sprint commitment and capacity
Help the product owner assess the feature's value against the current backlog items, evaluate the integration complexity, and make a transparent prioritization decision with stakeholder input

Approve the feature but extend the project timeline by three sprints to accommodate it without displacing any existing backlog items, requesting additional budget from the sponsor to cover the extension

Reject the feature because it was not in the original product vision and represents scope creep, directing the stakeholder to submit it as a separate project request through the portfolio intake process

data.stem: A project manager is overseeing a large enterprise transformation where three different department heads each believe their requirements should take top priority. Each department head has independently lobbied the CEO to prioritize their needs. The CEO has asked the project manager to resolve the competing priorities without further executive involvement. What is the most effective approach?
options: Create a weighted scoring model based on strategic alignment, financial impact, and urgency, then present the objective ranking to all three department heads simultaneously
Facilitate a prioritization workshop with all three department heads using agreed-upon criteria tied to organizational strategy, enabling a transparent and collaborative decision
Meet with each department head individually to understand their constraints and then make the prioritization decision independently based on the project manager's best judgment
Implement all three sets of requirements in parallel by adding resources to the project team to avoid the prioritization conflict
data.explanation: A facilitated workshop with transparent, strategy-linked criteria enables stakeholders to participate in the decision, increasing buy-in and alignment. This is the strongest stakeholder engagement approach. Option A presents a ranking but doesn't involve stakeholders in the process, reducing buy-in. Option B excludes stakeholders from the decision, which may create resistance. Option D avoids the conflict but likely increases cost, complexity, and risk.

data.stem: A project manager is planning a data migration project. The sponsor has set a firm deadline of six months, but the project manager's bottom-up estimate shows the work requires eight months. The project manager has already explored fast-tracking and crashing options, but fast-tracking introduces unacceptable data integrity risks and crashing exceeds the budget. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: The project manager must be transparent about the schedule gap and present options with trade-offs so the sponsor can make an informed decision. Option A accepts unrealistic constraints that will harm the team and likely still miss the deadline. Option C makes scope decisions without authorization and hides information from the sponsor. Option D is an overreaction when viable alternatives exist.
options: Accept the six-month deadline and plan to work overtime to meet it, absorbing the risk of team burnout while hoping that extended hours will close the gap between the estimated and required timeline

Present the sponsor with a transparent analysis showing the gap between the estimate and deadline, along with options such as phased migration, reduced scope, or deadline extension with associated trade-offs

Resign from the project since delivering in the required timeframe is not feasible with the current constraints, recommending the sponsor find a project manager willing to commit to the aggressive deadline
Commit to the six-month deadline and plan to descope lower-priority data sets without informing the sponsor, assuming the omission will not be noticed until after the migration deadline has passed

data.stem: A project team is using an AI-powered project management tool that automatically adjusts task priorities and resource allocations based on historical data. A team member raises a concern that the tool's recommendations consistently undervalue tasks assigned to remote workers. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: AI bias concerns require investigation and governance involvement. Option A is a workaround without addressing the root cause. Option C incorrectly assumes algorithms are inherently unbiased. Option D is an overreaction. Investigating, escalating, and implementing interim oversight addresses the concern systematically.
options: Stop using the AI tool entirely and return to manual project planning methods, eliminating any potential for algorithmic bias while accepting the loss of efficiency benefits
Investigate the concern by analyzing the tool's recommendation patterns, escalate findings to the AI governance team, and implement manual oversight until the issue is resolved
Override the tool's recommendations manually each sprint to ensure fair task distribution across all team members, negating the AI tool's optimization logic while maintaining its reporting features
Dismiss the concern since the tool uses objective data and algorithms cannot be biased by definition, reassuring the team member that mathematical models are inherently neutral and fair

data.stem: A project manager is leading a team that has just completed a major release. Before the next phase begins, several team members will rotate off the project and new members will join. The project manager wants to ensure continuity. What is the best approach to manage this transition?
data.explanation: Effective knowledge transfer requires multiple methods and interactive overlap. Working together allows tacit knowledge transfer that documentation alone cannot capture. Option A relies solely on written artifacts. Option C compresses transfer into a single event, risking information loss. Option D provides only one-way communication without the ability to ask questions.
options: Organize an overlap period where departing and incoming members work together, conduct structured knowledge transfer sessions, and update the project wiki with current context

Create comprehensive documentation of all processes, decisions, and lessons learned for new team members to read independently, relying solely on written materials as the primary knowledge transfer mechanism
Ask departing members to record video summaries of their responsibilities before they leave, providing the recordings as the sole onboarding resource for incoming team members
Schedule a single handoff meeting where departing members present their work to the incoming team, condensing all knowledge transfer into one session before the transition date

data.stem: A project manager is creating a procurement statement of work for a custom software development engagement. The business requirements are well understood, but the technical approach has several viable options that the vendor should evaluate. What type of procurement document should the project manager issue?
data.explanation: An RFP is appropriate when the buyer knows what they need (business requirements) but wants vendors to propose how to achieve it (technical approach). This allows evaluation of different approaches. Option A is for commodity purchases with clear specifications. Option B requires detailed technical specs the buyer does not yet have. Option D gathers information but does not solicit actual proposals.
options: Request for Proposal (RFP) that describes the business requirements and evaluation criteria, allowing vendors to propose their recommended technical approach
Request for Information (RFI) to gather market intelligence before deciding whether to proceed with procurement, which is exploratory and does not evaluate vendor proposals against criteria
Invitation for Bid (IFB) to solicit competitive bids based on detailed technical specifications, which assumes the solution is already fully defined and only price differentiation matters
Request for Quotation (RFQ) to get the lowest price from vendors for a well-defined deliverable, which focuses solely on cost comparison rather than evaluating vendor capabilities

data.stem: A project manager discovers that a key vendor for the project's cloud infrastructure has been acquired by a competitor. The contract has eighteen months remaining, and the vendor has assured continuity of service. However, the project manager is concerned about potential service disruptions, price changes, and intellectual property implications. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
data.explanation: The project manager should review contractual protections, assess the actual risk, and develop contingency plans — a measured, proactive response. Option A is an overreaction that could disrupt the project and incur termination costs. Option C is too passive given the material change in vendor ownership. Option D halts work unnecessarily before understanding the actual contractual and practical implications.
options: Continue with the current arrangement since the vendor has assured continuity and contractual obligations remain binding on the acquiring company under standard acquisition terms
Escalate to the legal department and halt all work dependent on this vendor until legal provides clearance, pausing deliverables regardless of the impact on the project schedule
Review the contract's change of control and termination clauses, assess the risk to the project, and develop a contingency plan while maintaining the vendor relationship
Terminate the contract immediately and begin procuring a replacement vendor to avoid future risk, even before understanding the acquiring company's intentions regarding existing contracts

data.stem: A project team has been working remotely for the duration of a six-month project. The project manager notices that informal team bonding is absent and collaboration happens only in formal meetings. Innovation and creative problem-solving have declined. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: Leading remote teams requires intentionally creating spaces for informal interaction and collaboration. Virtual social activities and dedicated brainstorming time can partially replicate the benefits of co-location. Option A may not be feasible or desirable. Option B increases meeting fatigue without addressing the informal interaction gap. Option D is defeatist and inaccurate.
options: Add more formal meetings to the schedule to increase interaction frequency, requiring mandatory attendance from all team members regardless of time zone or current workload priorities
Accept that remote teams are inherently less innovative and adjust project expectations accordingly, reducing the scope of creative deliverables to match the team's perceived limitations
Introduce virtual social activities, create informal communication channels, and allocate time for collaborative brainstorming sessions outside of regular status meetings
Require the team to return to the office to restore informal communication channels, mandating in-person attendance despite the established remote work arrangements and team preferences

data.stem: An agile team is working on a software product with sustainability requirements mandated by new regulations. The product owner wants to prioritize features that maximize user engagement, while the sustainability officer insists on prioritizing energy-efficient code optimization. The team has limited capacity for the next three sprints. What should the project manager facilitate?
options: Facilitate a collaborative session between the product owner and sustainability officer to create an integrated backlog that balances both regulatory compliance and business value
Split the team into two sub-teams with one focused on engagement features and the other on sustainability optimization
Prioritize user engagement features first since they deliver direct business value and address sustainability in a later release
Prioritize sustainability requirements first since regulatory non-compliance could result in fines that exceed the value of engagement features
data.explanation: The project manager should facilitate collaboration between stakeholders to find an integrated approach. Sustainability requirements tied to regulations are constraints, not optional features, but they must be balanced with business value delivery. Option A risks regulatory non-compliance. Option B ignores business value considerations. Option D fragments team capacity and likely reduces overall throughput for a small team.

data.stem: A project manager is overseeing a sustainability-focused initiative to reduce a manufacturing plant's carbon footprint by 30%. A key stakeholder, the plant operations director, has been passive during planning meetings and has not reviewed the draft implementation plan. The deadline for phase one is approaching. What should the project manager do?
options: Schedule a dedicated meeting with the operations director to understand their concerns and ensure alignment on the plan
Ask the project sponsor to mandate the operations director's participation
Proceed with the plan as drafted since the stakeholder had the opportunity to provide input
Assign a team member to summarize the plan and send it to the operations director for sign-off
data.explanation: Engaging stakeholders requires proactive, personal outreach, especially when a key stakeholder is disengaged. A one-on-one meeting helps surface concerns and build commitment. Option A risks resistance during execution. Option C undermines the relationship. Option D is passive and unlikely to secure genuine engagement.

data.stem: A Kanban team notices that their work-in-progress for the testing column has been at its limit of three items for two weeks, while the development column has two items below its WIP limit. Several completed development items are waiting to enter testing. What is the most appropriate action?
data.explanation: When a bottleneck is identified in Kanban, the team should swarm to address it while investigating root causes. Developers helping with testing improves immediate flow. Option A raises the WIP limit, which masks the bottleneck rather than resolving it. Option C bypasses quality assurance. Option D is a long-term staffing decision that does not address the immediate flow problem.
options: Increase the testing WIP limit to five to allow more items to flow through the testing column simultaneously, even though this may reduce focus and quality
Move items directly from development to done, skipping the testing column entirely to maintain flow, and address any quality issues discovered after release in production
Add two more testers to the team to permanently increase testing throughput, requesting additional headcount approval from the project sponsor to resolve the bottleneck
Have developers with available capacity swarm on the testing bottleneck to improve flow, while investigating the root cause of the testing constraint

data.stem: A project manager in a predictive environment is managing a dam construction project. A new environmental impact study reveals that the project's water diversion plan could harm a downstream ecosystem. The study was not part of the original environmental assessment. The project is 60% complete. What should the project manager do?
data.explanation: New environmental findings require proper investigation and governance. Option A ignores potentially serious environmental harm. Option C may be overly disruptive without understanding the full scope. Option D bypasses change control. An independent review with regulatory engagement and change control ensures a thorough, governed response.
options: Continue construction since the original environmental assessment was approved by regulators and remains legally valid until the regulatory body formally revokes it
Commission an independent review of the new study's findings, engage relevant environmental authorities, and initiate the change control process
Modify the water diversion plan based on the study's recommendations without formal change control, implementing the adjustments informally to avoid project delays
Immediately stop all construction activities until a new environmental impact assessment is completed and approved, regardless of the financial impact of the project delay

data.stem: A project manager is using an AI-powered risk analysis tool that has identified a pattern suggesting a 78% probability of a major vendor delay based on historical project data. The vendor's account manager assures the project manager that delivery will be on time. How should the project manager handle this situation?
data.explanation: Good risk management uses all available data sources. The AI prediction and vendor input are both valuable but neither is definitive. Adding it to the risk register, planning contingencies, and increasing monitoring is a balanced response. Option A ignores data-driven insight. Option B overreacts without verification. Option D is a disproportionate response to a risk that hasn't materialized.
options: Report the AI finding to the sponsor and recommend canceling the vendor contract immediately, replacing the vendor with an alternative supplier before the predicted delay materializes on the project
Acknowledge both inputs, add the potential delay to the risk register with the AI-assessed probability, develop a contingency plan, and increase monitoring of vendor progress milestones

Immediately find an alternative vendor based on the AI prediction to avoid the anticipated delay, initiating procurement without first validating the prediction's accuracy or discussing it with the current vendor

Trust the vendor's assurance since they have direct knowledge of their own operations and capacity, and disregard the AI prediction entirely as it lacks the contextual understanding of the vendor relationship
